<div class="markdown"><p>This notebook series is an intuitive introduction to the ideas in the paper: <a href="https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/pghzn_v3">Yu (2026), <em>The Art of Making Problems Simple: A Theory of Intelligence</em></a>. We expand on examples from <a href="https://probmods.org/">ProbMods</a> (Goodman, Tenenbaum &amp; The ProbMods Contributors) to build intuition for those ideas; the chapters do not follow the paper section by section. Full references are at the end of each notebook.</p><p>Chapter 1 of ProbMods, <a href="https://probmods.org/chapters/generative-models.html">Generative Models</a> (<a href="https://pluto.land/n/zlwvqg1g">Omega version</a>), begins with the idea of a working model: a model captures some useful structure in the world, and we can run it to imagine what might happen. A probabilistic program makes this idea concrete by describing a process that generates possible states of the world.</p><p>Once we have such a model, we can ask it many questions. We treat a <em>question</em> as a function</p><p class="tex">$$Q:\Omega\longrightarrow Y.$$</p><p>The input is a possible world <span class="tex">\(\omega\in\Omega\)</span>. The output <span class="tex">\(Q(\omega)\in Y\)</span> is the answer in that world. For example, a yes-or-no question has <span class="tex">\(Y=\{\mathsf{false},\mathsf{true}\}\)</span>, while a question about distance may return a real number. The <em>task</em> is to compute <span class="tex">\(Q(\omega)\)</span>.</p><p>A <em>representation</em> is a function</p><p class="tex">$$R:\Omega\longrightarrow Z$$</p><p>that describes a world in another space <span class="tex">\(Z\)</span>. Think of a subway map: the city is the "world", and the map represents it using stations and connections. The map supports questions such as "Can I travel from one station to another?" while discarding details such as building colours. Those details would matter for a different question, such as "What colour is the building above this station?"</p><p>In practice, a learner rarely sees the whole world. In the example below, it sees a sequence of coin flips but not which coin produced them. We write the observed part of a world as <span class="tex">\(x=\pi(\omega)\)</span>, and the questions and representations we build take that observation as input: <span class="tex">\(Q:X\to Y\)</span> and <span class="tex">\(R:X\to Z\)</span>.</p><p>A representation supports a question when a decoder <span class="tex">\(D_{QR}:Z\to Y\)</span> can recover the answer from it:</p><p class="tex">$$Q = D_{QR}\circ R.$$</p><p>Put another way, a representation decides which <em>distinctions</em> to keep. A decoder exists exactly when the question never separates two observations that the representation treats as the same.</p><p>This chapter asks which representation makes the answer to a question easy to compute. To study that, it separates three ingredients:</p><ol><li><p>a probabilistic model of possible worlds;</p></li><li><p>a question, and the task of computing its answer;</p></li><li><p>a representation that retains information for computing that answer.</p></li></ol></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Prerequisite:-Omega">Prerequisite: Omega</h2><p>Omega is a probabilistic programming language. A random variable is a function that takes a possible world <code>ω</code> and returns a value. The ProbMods <a href="https://pluto.land/n/zlwvqg1g">Generative Models</a> notebook introduces Omega in more detail; the few pieces this series uses are:</p><ul><li><p><code>@~ Bernoulli(p)</code> creates a new random variable with the given distribution. Each use of <code>@~</code> gives an independent random variable.</p></li><li><p><code>id ~ Bernoulli(p)</code> does the same with an explicit name <code>id</code>. Different names give independent random variables, so <code>(i ~ Bernoulli(p))(ω)</code> inside a loop over <code>i</code> draws a fresh value for each <code>i</code>. We use this for sequences of flips.</p></li><li><p><code>Variable(ω -&gt; ...)</code> builds a random variable from any function of the world, usually by combining other random variables evaluated in the same <code>ω</code>.</p></li><li><p><code>randsample(x, n)</code> evaluates <code>x</code> in <code>n</code> fresh worlds and returns the values.</p></li><li><p><code>x |ᶜ condition</code> conditions <code>x</code> on a Boolean random variable. We introduce it when we first use it below.</p></li></ul><p>The cell <code>ω = defω()</code> constructs a world, and <code>x(ω)</code> evaluates the Boolean random variable <code>x</code> in it. Run the cells below, then evaluate <code>x(ω)</code> again. It returns the same value in the same world. Try <code>x(defω())</code> or re-run the <code>ω = defω()</code> cell to evaluate it in a fresh world.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Example:-Learning-which-coin-produced-a-sequence">Example: Learning which coin produced a sequence</h2><p>Suppose a friend gives you a coin. It may be fair, or it may be a trick coin that lands heads 85% of the time. The program below first chooses which kind of coin your friend gave you and then generates a sequence of flips. After seeing the flips, we can ask which coin probably produced them.</p><p>The inference follows the coin example in ProbMods' <a href="https://probmods.org/chapters/learning-as-conditional-inference.html">Learning as conditional inference</a> (<a href="https://pluto.land/n/1nr1tmd6">Omega version</a>).</p></div>

```

```

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="What-different-representations-look-like">What different representations look like</h2><p>The full representation keeps the ordered <code>Vector{Bool}</code>. A smaller representation keeps only the sequence length and number of heads:</p><p>{HHHT, HHTH, HTHH} ──▶ (flips = 4, heads = 3)</p><p>For a fixed sequence length, the head count alone identifies the coordinate. Including <code>flips</code> lets the same representation handle sequences of different lengths.</p></div>

```julia
full_representation(sequence) = sequence
```

```julia
count_representation(sequence) = (
    flips = length(sequence),
    heads = count(identity, sequence),
)
```

```julia
[
    (sequence = show_sequence(sequence),
     alt_representation = count_representation(sequence))
    for sequence in [sequence_a, sequence_b]
]
```

```text
2-element Vector{@NamedTuple{sequence::String, alt_representation::@NamedTuple{flips::Int64, heads::Int64}}}:
 (sequence = "HHHT", alt_representation = (flips = 4, heads = 3))
 (sequence = "HTHH", alt_representation = (flips = 4, heads = 3))
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>The count representation treats many ordered observations as the same. A sequence of length <span class="tex">\(n\)</span> has <span class="tex">\(2^n\)</span> possible Boolean strings but only <span class="tex">\(n+1\)</span> possible head counts. For the present task, the smaller space keeps the distinction we need and removes distinctions that the model treats as irrelevant.</p></div>

```julia
function is_fair_posterior(sequence)
    sequence_likelihood(sequence, weight) =
        prod((s ? weight : 1 - weight) for s in sequence)
    fair_likelihood = sequence_likelihood(sequence, fair_weight)
    trick_likelihood = sequence_likelihood(sequence, trick_weight)
    fair_mass = is_fair_prior * fair_likelihood
    trick_mass = (1 - is_fair_prior) * trick_likelihood
    fair_mass / (fair_mass + trick_mass)
end
```

```julia
function count_decoder(representation)
    n = representation.flips
    k = representation.heads
    fair_likelihood = fair_weight^k * (1 - fair_weight)^(n - k)
    trick_likelihood = trick_weight^k * (1 - trick_weight)^(n - k)
    fair_mass = is_fair_prior * fair_likelihood
    trick_mass = (1 - is_fair_prior) * trick_likelihood
    fair_mass / (fair_mass + trick_mass)
end
```

```julia
[
    (
        sequence = show_sequence(sequence),
        task_from_full_sequence = is_fair_posterior(sequence),
        task_from_count = count_decoder(count_representation(sequence)),
    )
    for sequence in [sequence_a, sequence_b]
]
```

```text
2-element Vector{@NamedTuple{sequence::String, task_from_full_sequence::Float64, task_from_count::Float64}}:
 (sequence = "HHHT", task_from_full_sequence = 0.40422005739924816, task_from_count = 0.40422005739924816)
 (sequence = "HTHH", task_from_full_sequence = 0.40422005739924816, task_from_count = 0.40422005739924816)
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>For <code>HHHT</code> and <code>HTHH</code>, both columns should give about 0.404. <code>is_fair_posterior</code> multiplies the likelihood terms along the sequence. <code>count_decoder</code> groups those terms into powers using the head count. Both apply Bayes' rule: divide the fair coin's prior-weighted likelihood by the total for the two coin types.</p><p>Change the prior or either coin weight and compare the columns again. The values change together because both computations use the same model.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><p>The task computes the posterior probability that the coin is fair. Under this conditionally i.i.d. model, the likelihood has the form</p><p class="tex">$$P(s\mid\theta)=\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.$$</p><p>The likelihood depends on <span class="tex">\(n\)</span> and <span class="tex">\(k\)</span>, not on flip order. The decoder therefore recovers the exact task result from the count representation:</p><p class="tex">$$\mathsf{is\_fair\_posterior}
=
\mathsf{count\_decoder}\circ\mathsf{count\_representation}.$$</p><p>The head count is a sufficient statistic for this inference task under the assumed coin model.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Why-the-count-can-make-inference-cheaper">Why the count can make inference cheaper</h2><p>The two representations support different computations. Starting from an ordered sequence, <code>is_fair_posterior</code> multiplies one likelihood term for every flip, so it grows linearly with <span class="tex">\(n\)</span>. Starting from an already computed pair <span class="tex">\((n,k)\)</span>, <code>count_decoder</code> evaluates two likelihoods using powers and never traverses the observations. The cost of those powers depends on the arithmetic implementation, but the decoder avoids multiplying a separate likelihood term for every flip.</p><p>Computing <span class="tex">\(k\)</span> from a new sequence still requires one pass over the data. The first complete calculation is therefore <span class="tex">\(O(n)\)</span> in either representation. The saving appears when the learner stores the count, reuses it for later queries, or receives count data directly: the ordered representation occupies <span class="tex">\(O(n)\)</span> space and each new likelihood calculation scans <span class="tex">\(n\)</span> values, while the count representation occupies <span class="tex">\(O(1)\)</span> space and its decoder does not revisit the sequence.</p><p>The count also changes rejection sampling. Given a coin weight <span class="tex">\(\theta\)</span>, one particular ordered sequence with <span class="tex">\(k\)</span> heads has probability</p><p class="tex">$$\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k},$$</p><p>whereas the event "exactly <span class="tex">\(k\)</span> heads" has probability</p><p class="tex">$${n \choose k}\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.$$</p><p>The count-conditioned query therefore accepts <span class="tex">\({n \choose k}\)</span> times as many proposed worlds as a query conditioned on one particular ordering. The current implementation of the count query still generates all <span class="tex">\(n\)</span> flips in each proposed world, so the representation improves its acceptance rate but not the cost of generating one proposal. A generative model that represents the head count directly with a binomial random variable can also avoid constructing the ordered sequence when no task needs it.</p></div>

```julia
sequence_condition(observed) =
    Variable(ω -> flip_sequence(length(observed))(ω) == observed)
```

<div class="markdown"><p><code>sequence_condition</code> asks whether a generated sequence matches the observation.</p></div>

```julia
coin_given_sequence(observed::Vector) =
    is_fair_coin |ᶜ sequence_condition(observed)
```

<div class="markdown"><p><code>coin_given_sequence</code> uses <code>|ᶜ</code> to condition the coin type on that event.</p></div>

```julia
head_count_variable(n) = Variable(
    ω -> count(identity, flip_sequence(n)(ω))
)
```

```julia
coin_given_count(representation::NamedTuple) =
    is_fair_coin |ᶜ (ω -> head_count_variable(representation.flips)(ω) == representation.heads)
```

<div class="markdown"><p><code>coin_given_count</code> takes a count representation and matches only the number of heads.</p><p>The three sampling cells below therefore ask the same coin question using different representations of the data. Rejection sampling repeatedly draws a proposed world from the prior model: it chooses a coin type and generates flips from that coin. It keeps the coin type if the flips satisfy the observation condition and discards the proposal otherwise. The retained coin types are samples from the posterior. Averaging their Boolean values estimates the posterior probability that the coin is fair.</p></div>

```julia
posterior_a_samples = randsample(
    coin_given_sequence(sequence_a),
    400,
    alg = RejectionSample,
)
```

<div class="markdown"><p>The representation here matters because it exposes the symmetry of the model. Permuting the flips changes the raw sequence but leaves the inference coordinate unchanged.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Compare-the-number-of-proposed-worlds">Compare the number of proposed worlds</h2><p>The earlier calls each requested 400 <em>accepted posterior samples</em>. They did not fix how many worlds the sampler had to propose before finding those matches. To see the difference, we will generate a fixed collection of proposed worlds and apply both acceptance rules to that same collection. This setup makes the proposal and rejection steps explicit: each rule keeps matching worlds and discards the rest. Unlike the earlier calls, which stop after 400 acceptances, this experiment stops after a fixed number of proposals and counts how many each rule accepts.</p><p>Each proposal below contains a coin type and the sequence it generated. Both use the same <code>ω</code>, so the recorded coin type is the one that generated the flips. <code>proposal_count</code> controls how much work we allow before inspecting the estimates.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><p>For <code>HHHT</code>, the count rule should accept roughly four times as many proposals. It accepts <code>HHHT</code>, <code>HHTH</code>, <code>HTHH</code>, and <code>THHH</code>, while the sequence rule accepts only <code>HHHT</code>. Every sequence match is also a count match. Both conditions give the same posterior because the four orderings have equal likelihood under each coin.</p><p>Try <code>[true, true, false, false]</code> for <code>sequence_a</code>: the expected ratio becomes six. Try all heads: there is only one ordering, so the rules accept exactly the same proposals. Keep the sequence short while exploring; rare matches need many proposals.</p><p>The next cell compares estimates after different prefixes of the proposal stream. <code>estimate</code> averages the accepted coin types. A prefix with no accepted worlds returns <code>missing</code>, so increasing the sequence length does not produce a misleading zero estimate.</p></div>

```julia
function summarise_matches(proposals, matches)
    accepted = [world.fair for (world, keep) in zip(proposals, matches) if keep]
    n = length(accepted)
    p = is_fair_posterior(sequence_a)
    (accepted=n, estimate=n == 0 ? missing : mean(accepted),
     sampling_sd=n == 0 ? missing : sqrt(p * (1-p) / n))
end
```

```julia
[(proposed=n,
  sequence=summarise_matches(proposed_worlds[1:n], sequence_matches[1:n]),
  count=summarise_matches(proposed_worlds[1:n], count_matches[1:n]))
 for n in sort(unique(filter(n -> 0 < n <= proposal_count, proposal_budgets)))]
```

{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>As the proposal budget grows, both estimates approach the same fair-coin probability, about 0.404 at the starting settings. The count query collects more accepted samples from each prefix. Its estimate will usually fluctuate less, although a particular run can still put the sequence estimate closer to the answer.</p><p><code>sampling_sd</code> makes the accuracy comparison explicit. Accepted coin types are independent Boolean draws with the same posterior probability <span class="tex">\(p\)</span>. Conditional on accepting <span class="tex">\(m\)</span> worlds, their average has standard deviation <span class="tex">\(\sqrt{p(1-p)/m}\)</span>. We use the exact posterior from the earlier decoder to display that expected sampling variation. Four times as many accepted samples gives about half the standard deviation. This comparison describes variation across runs; individual estimates need not improve monotonically.</p><p>Rerun <code>proposed_worlds</code> and inspect the table again. Then raise <code>proposal_count</code> or change the observed sequence. The count representation's advantage is that it needs fewer proposals for a given accuracy.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Discussion">Discussion</h2><p>Change <code>sequence_b</code> while keeping its head count fixed. Which results stay the same, and which change? The count is useful for the coin question because the model makes flip order irrelevant once we know the coin type.</p><p>Now imagine a coin whose probability of heads depends on the previous flip. Would counting heads still preserve the posterior? What would you need to keep instead? Chapter 6 returns to such a coin and asks how a learner could tell it apart from the coin in this chapter.</p></div>
